source_title: 2023 ACC/AHA/ACCP/HRS Guideline for the Diagnosis and Management of Atrial Fibrillation (sections 7.2.1 Acute Rate Control, 7.2.2 Long-Term Rate Control, 10.12 Pulmonary Disease)
source_org_or_authors: Joglar JA, Chung MK, Armbruster AL, et al.; ACC/AHA Joint Committee on Clinical Practice Guidelines (with ACCP and HRS)
source_identifier: doi:10.1161/CIR.0000000000001193; PMID 38033089; PMC11095842 (full text read via NCBI efetch)
supporting_text: 7.2.2 rec 1 (COR 1, LOE B-NR): "In patients with AF, beta blockers or nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (diltiazem, verapamil) are recommended for long-term rate control with the choice of agent according to underlying substrate and comorbid conditions." 7.2.2 synopsis: "Selection of specific agents should consider patient-specific characteristics (ie, HFrEF, reactive airway disease) and response". 7.2.1 rec 1 (COR 1, LOE B-R): "In patients with AF with rapid ventricular response who are hemodynamically stable, beta blockers or nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (verapamil, diltiazem; provided that EF >40%) are recommended for acute rate control". 10.12 synopsis: "The combination of AF and asthma is less common, and beta blockers are generally avoided to prevent bronchospasm." 10.12 supportive text: "However, beta blockers can exacerbate reactive airway disease and are generally avoided in that setting, such as in patients with asthma."
simplifications: Metoprolol is chosen as the beta blocker, and diltiazem among the nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (verapamil is also listed).
The guideline's 'generally avoided' for beta blockers in asthma (synopsis and supportive text, not a numbered recommendation) is restated as a strict switch.
Applicability: only current asthma counts.

The guideline's limits on nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers are omitted: 7.2.1 rec 1 ('provided that EF >40%'), 7.2.1 rec 5 (COR 3: Harm, no intravenous ones with moderate or severe LV systolic dysfunction) and 7.2.2 rec 4 (COR 3: Harm, none with LVEF <40%). Other selection factors (heart failure, preexcitation, hemodynamic stability) are omitted too.
Acute and long-term rate control are not distinguished.
notes: VERIFIER: Re-extracted sections 7.2.1, 7.2.2 and 10.12 from the PMC full text: section numbers, quotes, COR and LOE all match (7.2.2 rec 1 COR 1/B-NR; 7.2.1 rec 1 COR 1/B-R; 10.12 rec 1 COR 2a/B-R). Changes: added the 7.2.2 synopsis quote and 7.2.1 rec 5, and located the 'LVEF <40%' harm recommendation precisely (7.2.2 rec 4, COR 3: Harm, LOE C-LD). LOPRESSOR SPL (Validus Pharmaceuticals LLC, DailyMed setid b5f4fed2-369c-4808-a682-8a5b8cfdbb4f, version 3, published 28 Jan 2026) confirmed: highlights 'Bronchospastic Disease: Avoid beta-blockers. (5.3)' and 5.3 'Patients with bronchospastic disease, should in general, not receive beta-blockers, including LOPRESSOR', which still allows cautious use when other antihypertensive treatment fails or is not tolerated; this label covers hypertension, angina and MI, not AF rate control. The same 2023 guideline (10.12 rec 1, COR 2a) calls cardioselective beta blockers reasonable in COPD, so the switch should not be read as covering COPD. 2014 AHA/ACC/HRS guideline (PMC4676081) confirmed: 'Non–beta-1 selective blockers, sotalol, propafenone, and adenosine are contraindicated in patients with bronchospasm' and 'Rate control can usually be achieved safely with nondihydropyridine calcium channel antagonists'. No contradictions found.

source_title: 2023 ACC/AHA/ACCP/HRS Guideline for the Diagnosis and Management of Atrial Fibrillation (sections 6.3 Oral Anticoagulants; 6.3.1 Antithrombotic Therapy, recommendation 2; 6.3.1.1; 6.8.5 AF in VHD)
source_org_or_authors: Joglar JA, Chung MK, Armbruster AL, et al.; ACC/AHA Joint Committee on Clinical Practice Guidelines (with ACCP and HRS)
source_identifier: doi:10.1161/CIR.0000000000001193; PMID 38033089; PMC11095842 (full text read via NCBI efetch)
supporting_text: 6.3.1 rec 2 (COR 1, LOE A): "In patients with AF who do not have a history of moderate to severe rheumatic mitral stenosis or a mechanical heart valve, and who are candidates for anticoagulation, DOACs are recommended over warfarin to reduce the risk of mortality, stroke, systemic embolism, and ICH." 6.3 (Vitamin K Antagonists): "Warfarin remains the first-line therapy in patients with AF and moderate-severe rheumatic mitral stenosis or mechanical heart valves." 6.8.5 synopsis: "VKAs are the anticoagulation drugs of choice for patients with rheumatic mitral stenosis, mechanical heart valves, and new-onset AF within 3 months after mechanical aortic or mitral valve surgery." 6.8.5 supportive text: "PROACT Xa (A Trial to Determine if Participants with an On-X Aortic Valve Can be Maintained Safely on Apixaban) was also terminated early due to higher thromboembolic events with apixaban in patients who were >3 months after mechanical On-X aortic valves."
simplifications: Apixaban is chosen among the DOACs.

The moderate-to-severe rheumatic mitral stenosis exception is omitted, as are the other reasons the guideline gives for warfarin in 6.3.1.1 (CYP3A4/P-glycoprotein-inducing drugs, cost or DOAC intolerance).
Applicability: only a current mechanical heart valve counts.
The anticoagulation indication is taken from the setting; the INR target is omitted.
notes: VERIFIER: Re-extracted 6.3, 6.3.1, 6.3.1.1 and 6.8.5 from the PMC full text. Corrected the attribution of the 'Warfarin remains the first-line therapy...' sentence: it is in section 6.3 (Vitamin K Antagonists), not 6.3.1. Added the 6.8.5 synopsis and the PROACT Xa sentence, which concerns apixaban specifically. 6.3.1.1 states: 'Warfarin remains the preferred agent in patients with AF receiving CYP3A4/p-glycoprotein–inducing agents, or moderate-severe mitral stenosis or mechanical heart valve.' ELIQUIS SPL (E.R. Squibb & Sons, L.L.C., DailyMed setid e9481622-7cc6-418a-acb6-c5450daae9b0, version 30, published 5 May 2025) confirmed: 5.4 'Patients with Prosthetic Heart Valves': 'The safety and efficacy of ELIQUIS have not been studied in patients with prosthetic heart valves. Therefore, use of ELIQUIS is not recommended in these patients.' Its 1.1 indication is limited to nonvalvular atrial fibrillation. 2014 AHA/ACC/HRS guideline (doi:10.1161/CIR.0000000000000041) confirmed: 'For patients with AF who have mechanical heart valves, warfarin is recommended...' and a Class III: Harm for dabigatran with a mechanical valve. The benchmark's past-tense templates describe a mechanical valve since replaced by a tissue valve, years earlier; apixaban for those is consistent with 6.8.5 rec 2 (COR 1, B-NR: DOACs over VKAs for valve disease other than moderate or greater mitral stenosis or a mechanical heart valve). No contradictions found.

source_title: American Geriatrics Society 2023 updated AGS Beers Criteria® for potentially inappropriate medication use in older adults
source_org_or_authors: 2023 American Geriatrics Society Beers Criteria® Update Expert Panel
source_identifier: J Am Geriatr Soc 2023;71(7):2052-2081; doi:10.1111/jgs.18372; PMID 37139824; full text opened at https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12478568/
supporting_text: Scope: 'The criteria are intended to be applied to adults 65 years old and older in all ambulatory, acute, and institutionalized settings of care, except hospice and end-of-life care settings.' Entry for non-COX-2-selective oral NSAIDs (naproxen is listed): 'Increased risk of GI bleeding or peptic ulcer disease in high-risk groups, including those >75 years old or taking oral or parenteral corticosteroids, anticoagulants, or antiplatelet agents; use of proton-pump inhibitor or misoprostol reduces but does not eliminate risk.' Recommendation: 'Avoid chronic use unless other alternatives are not effective and the patient can take a gastroprotective agent (proton-pump inhibitor or misoprostol). Avoid short-term scheduled use in combination with oral or parenteral corticosteroids, anticoagulants, or antiplatelet agents unless other alternatives are not effective and the patient can take a gastroprotective agent (proton-pump inhibitor or misoprostol).'
simplifications: The Beers scope (adults 65 years old and older) is recast as an explicit age criterion (65 years or more).
Co-medication narrowed to current aspirin. Beers names oral or parenteral corticosteroids, anticoagulants or antiplatelet agents.
Aspirin dose not specified. Beers treats low-dose aspirin as an antiplatelet agent but lists 'Aspirin >325 mg/day' itself among the non-COX-2-selective oral NSAIDs.
Gastroprotection narrowed to omeprazole. Beers allows a proton-pump inhibitor or misoprostol.
Precondition omitted: Beers says to avoid the NSAID unless other alternatives are not effective, but both branches of the rule prescribe naproxen directly.
Only the short-term scheduled-use criterion is reflected. The chronic-use criterion and the >75 high-risk group are not.
contradictions: Chronic use: Beers advises avoiding chronic NSAID use in every adult aged 65 or over unless alternatives are not effective and a gastroprotective agent is taken. For a patient aged 65+ who does not take aspirin (a base case for this all_of rule), the default 'naproxen alone' disagrees with Beers if the osteoarthritis treatment is ongoing. The rule agrees with Beers only for short-term scheduled use.
notes: VERIFIER: changes made: (1) Added the aspirin-dose simplification. (2) In the notes, replaced 'requires gastroprotection' with Beers' actual wording. Re-checked on 2026-10-02 against the PMC full text (PMC12478568, fetched through NCBI E-utilities): the scope sentence, and the Table 2 entry for non-COX-2-selective oral NSAIDs (naproxen listed; 'Aspirin >325 mg/day' also listed) with its rationale and both recommendation sentences, which match supporting_text. NICE NG226 1.4.4 was re-checked; the gastroprotection sentence is part of 1.4.4. The ACG 2009 full text returned HTTP 402 and was not opened. STOPP/START version 3 (O'Mahony et al., Eur Geriatr Med 2023;14(4):625-632, PMID 37256475, PMC10447584) was opened, but its criteria list is in supplementary material that was not opened, so it was not checked as a closer source. Researcher's notes (adjusted): The author left no source note (grammar_curated all_of family), so the source was identified by content match. Beers applies to adults aged 65 and older. It advises avoiding short-term scheduled use of an oral NSAID with an antiplatelet agent such as aspirin, unless other alternatives are not effective and the patient can take a gastroprotective agent. The classification is borderline between simplified_source and synthetic because the rule keeps only the short-term criterion. Another source disagrees with the default 'naproxen alone' at any age: NICE NG226 (published 19 October 2022) 1.4.4 says 'Offer a gastroprotective treatment (such as a proton pump inhibitor) for people with osteoarthritis while they are taking an NSAID.' The ACG 2009 NSAID-ulcer guideline (Lanza FL, Chan FK, Quigley EM; Am J Gastroenterol 2009;104:728-738; doi:10.1038/ajg.2009.115; PMID 19240698) was confirmed to exist, but its full text could not be opened, so its risk-factor list is not used. Checked 2026-10-02.

contradictions: Patients under 75 with eGFR 30-44 (vs Glucophage SmPC): the SmPC maximum is 1000 mg/day at any age, but the rule keeps 1000 mg twice daily (2000 mg/day).

eGFR below 30 (vs Glucophage SmPC): the SmPC contraindicates metformin ('Severe renal failure (GFR < 30 mL/min)'), but the rule still prescribes it (500 mg twice daily at 75 or more, 1000 mg twice daily otherwise).
notes: VERIFIER: no field changed; both contradictions hold. Re-checked on 2026-10-02: the Glucophage SmPC, eMC 987 ('GLUCOPHAGE 500 mg film-coated tablets' and 'GLUCOPHAGE 850 mg film-coated tablets'; Merck; last updated on emc 22 Dec 2025; date of revision November 2025). Checked: the 4.2 renal table (60-89: 3000 mg; 45-59: 2000 mg; 30-44: 1000 mg; <30: 'Metformin is contraindicated'), the 'Elderly' sentence and 4.3 'Severe renal failure (GFR < 30 mL/min)'. The researcher's search for a source that makes the dose depend on age 75 was not repeated in full; one generic web search found no such source. Researcher's notes (kept): Benchmark composition (grammar_curated all_of family; no author note). The eGFR condition and both doses match the metformin SmPC renal table, but no source was found that also makes the dose reduction depend on age 75 or more (searched, including Japanese guidance). The table of 'GFR (mL/min)' against 'Total maximum daily dose' gives: 60-89, 3000 mg; 45-59, 2000 mg; 30-44, 1000 mg; <30, 'Metformin is contraindicated'. It also says: 'Elderly: Due to the potential for decreased renal function in elderly subjects, the metformin dosage should be adjusted based on renal function.' The rule's default (1000 mg twice daily = 2000 mg/day) equals the 45-59 maximum, and its alternative (500 mg twice daily = 1000 mg/day) equals the 30-44 maximum. The SmPC uses GFR in mL/min; the rule uses eGFR in mL/min/1.73 m2.

contradictions: Trigger for the reduced dose (vs ALDACTONE US label): the label lowers the starting regimen on eGFR alone ('between 30 and 50'; 25 mg once daily requires eGFR >50). The rule also requires potassium above 4.8 mmol/L, so a patient with eGFR 40 and potassium 4.5 gets 25 mg daily under the rule. At eGFR exactly 50, the rule gives 25 mg daily whatever the potassium.

Potassium above 5.0 (vs label): 25 mg once daily is the label's starting dose only when serum potassium is ≤5.0 mEq/L, and hyperkalemia is a contraindication. The UK Aldactone SmPC also lists hyperkalaemia under 4.3 and says to discontinue or interrupt treatment for serum potassium >5 mEq/L. The rule prescribes spironolactone whatever the potassium: 25 mg daily when eGFR is 50 or more, and 12.5 mg daily when eGFR is below 50 (e.g. potassium 5.6 mmol/L).
Regimen (vs label): the label's reduced regimen is 25 mg every other day, not 12.5 mg daily.

eGFR below 30: the US label gives no heart-failure starting regimen below eGFR 30. The UK Aldactone SmPC contraindicates 'acute renal insufficiency, significant renal compromise, anuria', without a numeric definition. The rule prescribes spironolactone at any eGFR (12.5 mg daily when potassium is above 4.8 mmol/L, otherwise 25 mg daily).
notes: VERIFIER: changes made: (1) Contradiction 2 now also covers eGFR below 50, because the rule's 12.5 mg branch includes potassium above 5.0; it also cites the UK SmPC. (2) The eGFR-50 boundary was added to contradiction 1. (3) The UK SmPC was added to contradiction 4. Re-checked on 2026-10-02: US ALDACTONE SPL setid 0fed2822-3a03-4b64-9857-c682fcd462bc (Pfizer Laboratories Div Pfizer Inc; version 25, effective 2025-11-28), sections 1.1, 2.2 and 4 as quoted. UK Aldactone 25 mg Film-Coated Tablets SmPC (Pfizer Limited, eMC product 1619; last updated on emc 02 Feb 2026; date of revision 01/2026), 4.2: treatment 'should be initiated at a dose of spironolactone 25 mg once daily if serum potassium is ≤5.0 mEq/L and serum creatinine is ≤2.5 mg/dL', and patients who do not tolerate it 'may have their dose reduced to 25 mg every other day'. Its 4.3 and 4.4 are as cited above. The ACC/AHA guideline pages (ahajournals.org, jacc.org, sciencedirect.com) returned HTTP 403 or a captcha. A search-result snippet from the AHFS monograph on drugs.com (page not opened: HTTP 403) attributes an initial '12.5 mg once daily or every other day' for eGFR 30-49 mL/min/1.73 m2 to ACCF/AHA. This is unverified and not used. Researcher's notes (kept): Benchmark composition (grammar_curated all_of family; no author note). Searching found no source that uses a potassium cut-off of 4.8 mmol/L for spironolactone dosing. ALDACTONE US label, 2.2 Treatment of Heart Failure: 'In patients with serum potassium ≤5.0 mEq/L and eGFR >50 mL/min/1.73 m2, initiate treatment at 25 mg once daily. ... In patients with an eGFR between 30 and 50 mL/min/1.73 m2, consider initiating therapy at 25 mg every other day because of the risk of hyperkalemia.' Section 4 lists hyperkalemia as a contraindication, and the heart-failure indication is NYHA class III-IV heart failure with reduced ejection fraction. Because the ACC/AHA dosing tables could not be opened, it could not be checked whether they list 12.5 mg daily for reduced eGFR, and no guideline is relied on for the 12.5 mg dose.

contradictions: eGFR below 30 branch (vs UK colchicine SmPC). The Colchicine 500 microgram Tablets SmPC (Strides Pharma UK, eMC product 14362) lists 'Patients with severe renal impairment' under 4.3 Contraindications. It also says colchicine 'should not be used in patients undergoing haemodialysis'. The switch to colchicine therefore conflicts with UK labelling. The SmPC gives no numeric definition of severe renal impairment; the US COLCRYS label defines severe renal failure as CrCl less than 30 mL/min. Unlike the UK SmPC, COLCRYS allows treatment of gout flares in severe renal impairment without dose adjustment, with courses repeated no more than once every two weeks, and a single 0.6 mg dose on dialysis.

Ulcer branch (vs Naprosyn EC SmPC): 4.3 also contraindicates a history of peptic ulceration ('two or more distinct episodes of proven ulceration or bleeding') and 'History of gastrointestinal bleeding or perforation, related to previous NSAIDs therapy'. The rule counts only an active ulcer, so a patient with recurrent past ulcers or a past NSAID-related bleed, and no active ulcer, gets naproxen under the rule. This affects the benchmark's time near-misses: they describe a past or resolved ulcer and are labelled naproxen.
notes: VERIFIER: changes made: (1) The EULAR remark was corrected: the abstract does mention renal function, but only for allopurinol dosing, and it does not address flare treatment in renal impairment. (2) Contradiction 2 now includes the SmPC's second GI clause (past NSAID-related bleeding or perforation). (3) Contradiction 1 now includes the haemodialysis clause, the lack of a numeric definition in the UK SmPC and the COLCRYS CrCl definition. (4) The COLCRYS SPL that was opened is now recorded. Re-checked on 2026-10-02: Colchicine SmPC eMC 14362 (Strides Pharma UK Ltd; last updated on emc 26 Feb 2026; date of revision 29/01/2026), 4.2 and 4.3. Naprosyn EC 375 mg SmPC eMC 13240 (Atnahs Pharma UK Ltd; last updated on emc 07 Oct 2024; date of revision 07/08/2024), 4.2 and 4.3. US naproxen SPL setid 86a3e612-3bfe-432f-9afd-972bb8a6644e (American Health Packaging; version 6, published 28 Sep 2026), 8.7. COLCRYS SPL setid d6adc880-5499-4691-93f3-27c87902d5fc (repackager Proficient Rx LP; version 4, effective 2022-10-01), 2.5 and 8.6; a DailyMed search for 'colcrys' returned only repackager SPLs. NICE NG219 1.3.1 and 1.3.2 ('Consider adding a proton pump inhibitor for people with gout who are taking an NSAID to treat a gout flare'). NICE CKS (gout) and the BNF are available only in the UK and could not be opened, so a single source combining these conditions could not be ruled out there. Researcher's notes (corrected): No single source states this switch. The rule is a benchmark composition (grammar_curated any_of family; no author note): both conditions are naproxen contraindications, and the alternative is one of NICE's first-line options. The Naprosyn EC 375 mg SmPC says in 4.3: 'Active or history of peptic ulceration or active gastrointestinal bleeding (two or more distinct episodes of proven ulceration or bleeding)', and in 4.2: 'Naproxen is contraindicated in patients with baseline creatinine clearance less than 30 ml/minute'. US naproxen labeling says in 8.7 that naproxen-containing products are 'not recommended for use in patients with moderate to severe and severe renal impairment (creatinine clearance <30 mL/min)'. NICE NG219 (published 09 June 2022) 1.3.1 says 'Offer a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID), colchicine or a short course of an oral corticosteroid for first-line treatment of a gout flare, taking into account the person's comorbidities, co-prescriptions and preferences'. NG219 does not rank the three options. The rule uses eGFR (mL/min/1.73 m2) where the labels use creatinine clearance (mL/min). For the EULAR 2016 gout recommendations (Richette et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2017;76:29-42, PMID 27457514), the full text returned HTTP 403, so their advice is not used.

Consider nifedipine for women in whom labetalol is not suitable, or methyldopa if both labetalol and nifedipine are not suitable'. For gestational hypertension, 1.4.5 names the same three drugs in the same order. Amlodipine is not among them; NG133 mentions amlodipine only for the postnatal period (1.9.5, 1.9.6).

Default (vs NICE NG136 1.4.35 and 1.4.30): at step 1, adults aged 55 or over, or of Black African or African-Caribbean family origin, without type 2 diabetes are offered a calcium-channel blocker, not an ACE inhibitor. 1.4.30 also says to consider an ARB in preference to an ACE inhibitor for adults of Black African or African-Caribbean family origin. The rule prescribes lisinopril to every patient who meets neither listed condition.
notes: VERIFIER: changes made: (1) The potassium item was moved from contradictions to notes (point 2 below). Its direction agrees with the only cut-off found, NG203 1.6.16, so it extends a CKD recommendation to all adults without support but does not disagree with any source. (2) The pregnancy contradiction now also cites NG133 1.4.5 (gestational hypertension: same three drugs, no amlodipine) and the numbers of the postnatal recommendations. (3) The default contradiction now also cites NG136 1.4.30. (4) The lisinopril SPL's labeler and version and NG203's last-updated date were added. Researcher's notes (corrected): No single source was found that pairs these two conditions with a switch from lisinopril to amlodipine. (1) Pregnancy: the ZESTRIL (lisinopril) US label boxed warning says 'When pregnancy is detected, discontinue ZESTRIL as soon as possible'. Label details: DailyMed setid 838c2d78-d2d8-4981-9ec9-e50ef9e1a5d8, labeler Upsher-Smith Laboratories, LLC, SPL version 2 effective 2025-01-02, 'Revised 11/2024'. source_title: 2012 American College of Rheumatology guidelines for management of gout. Part 1: systematic nonpharmacologic and pharmacologic therapeutic approaches to hyperuricemia (Table 3)
source_org_or_authors: American College of Rheumatology (Khanna D, FitzGerald JD, Khanna PP, et al.)
source_identifier: Arthritis Care Res (Hoboken) 2012;64(10):1431-1446, doi:10.1002/acr.21772, PMID 23024028, PMC3683400 (full text opened)
supporting_text: Table 3: "A. ALLOPURINOL: Starting dose should be no greater than 100 mg/day for any patient, and start at 50 mg/day in stage 4 or worse CKD (Evidence B)". Key points: "The starting dose of allopurinol should be no greater than 100 mg per day, and less than that in moderate to severe chronic kidney disease (CKD), followed by gradual upwards titration of the maintenance dose, which can exceed 300 mg daily even in patients with CKD".
simplifications: The 100 mg/day ceiling ('no greater than') is restated as a fixed 100 mg daily dose. The source's figures are starting doses; the rule text does not say 'starting'.

'Stage 4 or worse CKD' is restated as eGFR below 30 mL/min/1.73 m2, the standard GFR boundary of stage 4. The ACR text does not state this mapping: it never mentions eGFR or GFR and discusses creatinine clearance.
Upward titration of the maintenance dose every 2-5 weeks (which can exceed 300 mg daily even in CKD), HLA-B*5801 screening and flare prophylaxis are omitted.
contradictions: Partial; the source contradicts itself. ACR 2012's Key points say the starting dose should be 'less than that in moderate to severe chronic kidney disease (CKD)'. Its Table 3 and text set the lower start (50 mg/day) at 'stage 4 or worse CKD'. The rule follows Table 3. ACR 2020 defines moderate-to-severe CKD as stage ≥3. Under the Key points wording, base cases at eGFR 45-59 and near-misses at eGFR 30-35 would start below 100 mg, where the rule labels 100 mg correct.
notes: VERIFIER: Confirmed the identifiers and the Table 3 quote verbatim (PMC3683400). Changes: (1) added a partial contradiction: the source's own Key points are broader than its Table 3. (2) Corrected the researcher's claim that the 2020 guideline gives no 50 mg figure. Its text says 'Even lower initial allopurinol doses (e.g., ≤50 mg/day) should be considered in patients with CKD.' It gives no stage 4 or eGFR 30 cut-off. (3) Restored the ≤ and ≥ symbols in quotations and tightened the case ranges using selrm/rules_constraint.py and selrm/engine.py. Researcher notes re-checked: the 2020 ACR guideline (FitzGerald JD et al., Arthritis Care Res 2020;72(6):744-760, doi:10.1002/acr.24180, PMID 32391934, PMC10563586; full text opened) supersedes 2012. It strongly recommends 'Starting treatment with low-dose allopurinol (≤100 mg/day and lower in patients with CKD [stage ≥3])'. Under it, base cases at eGFR 45-59 and near-misses at eGFR 30-35 would also start below 100 mg. The alt-tier threshold (60) corresponds to that stage ≥3 boundary. Flip values are eGFR 15-29 (stage 4 only).

source_title: EHA Guidelines on Management of Antithrombotic Treatments in Thrombocytopenic Patients With Cancer (HemaSphere 2022;6(8):e750)
source_org_or_authors: European Hematology Association; Falanga A, Leader A, Ambaglio C, Bagoly Z, et al.
supporting_text: Recommendations 5 (therapeutic-dose anticoagulation): "b. Grade 3 TP: i. We recommend against using DOACs and VKAs for VTE and AF. Level 5, grade D ii. LMWH, at doses either prophylactic or therapeutic reduced by 50%, should be used in patients with acute VTE, after balancing bleeding and thrombosis risk. Level 2b, grade C"; "c. Grade 4 TP: We recommend holding anticoagulant drugs for all the indications. Level 2b, grade C"; "d. Grade 3–4 TP: In case of very-high-thrombotic risk, we suggest continuing anticoagulation and increase platelet counts by platelet transfusion or use of TPO-RA"; "a. Grade 1–2 TP: i. We recommend therapeutic-dose parenteral or oral anticoagulation according to the approved indications after a careful evaluation of bleeding and thrombotic risk in the individual patient." Table 2 (x10^9/L): Grade 3 "<50 to 25", Grade 4 "<25".
simplifications: Thrombocytopenia grades 3 (25 to <50) and 4 (<25) collapsed into one threshold, <50 x10^9/L.
LMWH narrowed to enoxaparin. The source's dose (prophylactic, or therapeutic reduced by 50%, in grade 3) is omitted.

The very-high-thrombotic-risk options for grades 3-4 are omitted. Rec 5d: continue anticoagulation with platelet transfusion or TPO-RA. The rule does not mention MRSA or the outpatient setting.
Alternative chosen among the remaining listed options: doxycycline.

The label's caution (increased methotrexate toxicity, rare megaloblastic pancytopenia) and the regulator's advice (avoid whenever possible; if the combination cannot be avoided, warn patients about bone marrow suppression) are restated as an unconditional switch.
Applicability restated as current methotrexate use only; methotrexate dose and indication are not distinguished.

contradictions: The methotrexate labels also list tetracyclines as interacting drugs, so they do not support doxycycline as an interaction-free substitute. The Nordimet SmPC (4.5) says tetracyclines 'displace methotrexate from serum albumin binding and thus increase bioavailability (indirect dose increase)' and that oral tetracyclines 'may reduce intestinal methotrexate absorption or interfere with the enterohepatic circulation'. The current US methotrexate tablets label (Revised 05/2026, 7.1) lists 'Highly protein-bound drugs (e.g., oral anticoagulants, phenytoin, salicylates, sulfonamides, sulfonylureas, and tetracyclines)' alongside sulfonamide antibiotics under 'If coadministration cannot be avoided, monitor closely'. Neither label tells prescribers to avoid tetracyclines, so this concerns the choice of alternative, not the direction of the switch. No source found says doxycycline should replace TMP-SMX in methotrexate users.

The indication differs from IDSA 2014, the guideline named in the rule's source note and the one IDSA lists as Current. After incision and drainage, that guideline ties antibiotics to SIRS ('moderate' purulent infection = 'purulent infection with systemic signs of infection'). In its Figure 1, a drained abscess with surrounding cellulitis and no systemic signs is 'Mild' (I & D only). The 'associated cellulitis' trigger comes from IDSA 2011, where it is qualified by 'rapid progression', and IDSA's guideline index lists that 2011 MRSA guideline as Archived.

Oral agent chosen among the four Figure 1 options (cephalexin, as the cephalosporin); intravenous agent chosen among four options (cefazolin). Table 2 names both.

Severe tier and MRSA risk factors omitted: failed oral therapy, immunocompromise, signs of deeper infection or organ dysfunction, penetrating trauma, MRSA infection or colonization, injection drug use.

Units restated: 12 000 cells/µL becomes 12.0 x10^9/L. The Figure 1 legend as printed reads '(<12 000 or <400 cells/µL)'; the 2015 correction (doi:10.1093/cid/civ114) changes it to '(>12 000 or <4000 cells/µL)'. The code comment's 'two or more' SIRS criteria is not in IDSA 2014. Recommendation 6 lists the SIRS signs joined by 'or', and neither the executive summary nor the full guideline text on the IDSA site defines SIRS as two or more criteria.
contradictions: IDSA is internally inconsistent, and the rule follows only one reading. Recommendation 14 classes cellulitis with SIRS as 'severe nonpurulent' and recommends vancomycin or another agent effective against both MRSA and streptococci. Fever plus leukocytosis meets the two-or-more SIRS reading in the code comment, yet the rule prescribes intravenous cefazolin. That matches Figure 1's moderate tier ('systemic signs of infection'), not recommendation 14.

Interpretation-dependent: IDSA joins the systemic signs with 'or' and gives no count. In this all_of rule the generator holds the non-target criterion met (selrm/engine.py, pivots and _propose), so every base and near-miss case shows exactly one sign. Either the temperature is 38.4-38.8 C with a white cell count below threshold, or the white cell count is 12.6-13.6 x10^9/L without fever. If one sign counts as 'systemic signs of infection', IDSA rates these cases at least moderate: intravenous therapy under Figure 1, or severe under recommendation 14 if recommendation 6's 'or' definition of SIRS is applied. The rule gives oral cephalexin. Under the two-or-more SIRS reading the rule agrees (recommendation 18: outpatient therapy for patients who do not have SIRS).

(I, B); 'Ticagrelor is recommended irrespective of the treatment strategy (invasive or conservative) (180 mg LD, 90 mg b.i.d. MD).' (I, B); 'Prasugrel should be considered in preference to ticagrelor for ACS patients who proceed to PCI.' (IIa, B); 'In older ACS patients, especially if HBR, clopidogrel as the P2Y12 receptor inhibitor may be considered.' (III, B) || Recommendation Table 15: 'It is recommended to apply the same diagnostic and therapeutic strategies in patients with CKD (dose adjustment may be necessary) as in patients with normal kidney function.' || ARC-HBR (Urban 2019): 'Twenty clinical criteria were identified as major or minor by consensus' || 'Patients are considered to be at HBR if at least 1 major or 2 minor criteria are met.' || 'sufficient data are not currently available to create a point-based score that would take into account the relative weight of each HBR criterion' || 'Age ≥75 years is considered a minor ARC-HBR criterion' || 'Severe or end-stage chronic kidney disease (CKD; estimated glomerular filtration rate [eGFR] <30 mL/min) is considered a major ARC-HBR criterion, and moderate CKD (eGFR, 30–59 mL/min) is considered a minor ARC-HBR criterion' || 'Spontaneous (nonintracranial) bleeding requiring hospitalization or transfusion in the past 6 months (or at any time if recurrent) is considered a major ARC-HBR criterion, and a first spontaneous (nonintracranial) bleed requiring hospitalization or transfusion >6 and <12 months before PCI is considered a minor ARC-HBR criterion' || ARC-HBR Table 3 (EHJ version), major column: 'Severe or end-stage CKD (eGFR <30 mL/min)', 'Previous spontaneous ICH (at any time)', 'Previous traumatic ICH within the past 12 mo'; minor column: 'Age ≥75 y', 'Spontaneous bleeding requiring hospitalization or transfusion within the past 12 mo not meeting the major criterion'
simplifications: ARC-HBR defines HBR as a yes/no test (≥1 major or ≥2 minor criteria) and states that 'sufficient data are not currently available to create a point-based score'. The rule turns this into points: major = 2, minor = 1, cutoff 2.

Only 3 of the 20 ARC-HBR criteria are used. The rest are left out, for example expected long-term oral anticoagulation, anaemia, thrombocytopenia, recent ischaemic stroke, active malignancy, recent major surgery or trauma, and long-term NSAID or steroid use.

Criteria with two levels are cut to one. CKD (eGFR <30 is major, 30-59 is minor) becomes eGFR <30 only. Prior bleeding (major within 6 months or if recurrent, minor for a first bleed >6 and <12 months ago) becomes a single 'major bleeding event at any time' item.

The bleeding item is reworded. ARC-HBR counts spontaneous (nonintracranial) bleeding requiring hospitalisation or transfusion, and lists intracranial haemorrhage separately (previous spontaneous ICH at any time and previous traumatic ICH within the past 12 months, both major). The rule says only 'a major bleeding event', does not require it to be spontaneous, and folds intracranial bleeds into the same item.

ARC-HBR's kidney criterion is severe or end-stage chronic kidney disease. The rule uses a single current eGFR value, so an acute fall below 30 counts under the rule although it is not chronic kidney disease.
Units: ARC-HBR gives eGFR <30 mL/min (in the text and in Table 3), while the rule uses mL/min/1.73 m2.

One default is picked from the potent P2Y12 inhibitors. ESC 2023 recommends prasugrel (I B for P2Y12-inhibitor-naive patients proceeding to PCI) or ticagrelor (I B), and says prasugrel should be considered in preference to ticagrelor for ACS patients who proceed to PCI (IIa B). The rule uses ticagrelor.

Optional guidance becomes a direct instruction. ESC 2023 says clopidogrel should only be used, among other cases, 'in some patients considered otherwise at HBR', and that it 'may be considered' (IIb B) in older patients, especially with HBR. The rule switches every patient at or above the cutoff to clopidogrel, and does not offer the other HBR strategies in ESC 2023 Recommendation Table 6 (1-month DAPT then monotherapy; de-escalation).
ESC 2023's separate option of clopidogrel for older patients (e.g. ≥70 years) without HBR is not reflected: age ≥75 alone scores 1, below the cutoff.
DAPT duration is not stated: ESC 2023 recommends a P2Y12 receptor inhibitor in addition to aspirin for 12 months unless there is HBR.
contradictions: eGFR <30 mL/min is a major ARC-HBR criterion and is enough on its own for HBR, but the rule scores it 1 point. A patient whose only criterion is eGFR <30 is HBR under ARC-HBR, the definition ESC 2023 adopts, yet scores 1 (<2) under the rule. The conflict is in the weighting. ESC 2023 still allows the drug the rule gives this patient (ticagrelor), because it makes clopidogrel for HBR optional ('in some patients considered otherwise at HBR') and says to apply the same therapeutic strategies in CKD.

Prior bleeding at any time scores 2 points under the rule, enough on its own. Under ARC-HBR, a spontaneous non-intracranial bleed is major only within the past 6 months or if recurrent, is minor if it was within the past 12 months, and does not count if older; bleeds that were not spontaneous are not a bleeding criterion. Take a patient whose only finding is a single spontaneous non-intracranial bleed more than 6 months ago, or a non-spontaneous non-intracranial bleed (with no other criterion, such as major surgery or trauma within 30 days before PCI). The rule switches this patient to clopidogrel, but the patient is not HBR under ARC-HBR, and ESC 2023 says clopidogrel 'should only be used when prasugrel or ticagrelor are contraindicated/not available, or in some patients considered otherwise at HBR'. For a previous spontaneous intracranial haemorrhage the rule agrees with the source, because ARC-HBR counts it as major at any time.
notes: VERIFIER: Checked ESC 2023 in the ORBi PDF (section 6.1.1 text, Recommendation Tables 5, 6 and 15, and Table 6). Checked ARC-HBR in the Circulation full text (Europe PMC) and in the EHJ co-publication, which has Table 3 as text. PubMed confirms all identifiers. Every quote matches, including the section and table numbers. Changes: (1) Read ARC-HBR Table 3 in the EHJ version of the same consensus document. It gives 'eGFR <30 mL/min', so the units simplification stands; it has 14 major and 6 minor criteria (20, as the text says); and it lists intracranial haemorrhage as separate major criteria. Added the EHJ record to source_identifier and the Table 3 rows to supporting_text. (2) Added simplifications: ICH and the 'spontaneous' condition folded into one bleeding item; chronic kidney disease replaced by a current eGFR value; DAPT duration not stated; prasugrel's class I B for P2Y12-naive patients going to PCI. Removed 'previous intracranial haemorrhage' from the list of omitted criteria, since the rule's bleeding item covers it. (3) Narrowed the bleeding contradiction to a single spontaneous non-intracranial bleed more than 6 months ago and to bleeds that were not spontaneous. For previous spontaneous ICH the rule agrees with ARC-HBR. (4) Added to the eGFR contradiction that ESC 2023 still allows the drug the rule gives (ticagrelor), so the conflict is the weight, not the drug. ESC Table 6 also says 'no specific dose adjustment in CKD patients' for ticagrelor. ESC Table 6 lists prior stroke as a contraindication for prasugrel but gives no intracranial-haemorrhage contraindication for ticagrelor; the ticagrelor drug label was not checked. Kept: provenance, sources and the other simplifications. Retained researcher notes: ESC 2023 adopts ARC-HBR for HBR. The ESC footnote points to an ARC-HBR table in Supplementary section 8.2.2.3, which was not opened. The 2/1/1 weights with cutoff 2 reproduce 'one major or two minor' for age (minor) and for recent or recurrent bleeding (major), but not for eGFR <30 (major). Timing caveat: ESC 2023 says 'De-escalation of antiplatelet therapy in the first 30 days after an ACS event is not recommended' (III B). It also says de-escalation from prasugrel or ticagrelor to clopidogrel 'may be considered as an alternative DAPT strategy to reduce bleeding risk' (IIb A). The rule is read as the first choice of P2Y12 inhibitor. If a patient on the ward had already had a ticagrelor loading dose at PCI, switching to clopidogrel within 30 days would be that kind of de-escalation.

contradictions: Relative to qSOFA, where the three criteria come from (it is not a source for this rule): qSOFA gives each criterion 1 point and flags a score of 2 or more (Seymour 2016; Singer 2016). The rule gives respiratory rate ≥22/min 2 points and needs 3, so tachypnoea is required. A patient with altered mentation and systolic BP ≤100 mmHg but respiratory rate <22/min is qSOFA-positive (2 points), yet scores 2 (<3) under the rule and stays on oral amoxicillin. Every other combination of the three criteria splits the same way as qSOFA ≥2.
notes: VERIFIER: Checked every claim. PubMed confirms Seymour 2016 (doi:10.1001/jama.2016.0288, PMID 26903335, PMC5433435), Singer 2016 (doi:10.1001/jama.2016.0287, PMID 26903338, PMC4968574) and SSC 2021 (doi:10.1007/s00134-021-06506-y, PMID 34599691, PMC8486643). The qSOFA quotes are in the Seymour abstract and the Singer full text, and the SSC 2021 quote is its recommendation 2. NICE NG250 (Pneumonia: diagnosis and management, published 2 September 2025; recommendations page re-fetched 2026-10-02) says what the researcher reports. No field changed. Synthetic is right: no source maps these criteria, or qSOFA, to oral amoxicillin versus IV piperacillin-tazobactam, and the weights and cutoff are not qSOFA's. The contradiction entry is kept on purpose. It records the divergence from qSOFA, the published criteria set the rule borrows (not its source), and it is correct: a score of 3 or more is the same as 'respiratory rate ≥22/min AND (altered mentation OR systolic BP ≤100 mmHg)'. Added to notes: (1) NG250 Table 3 makes oral co-amoxiclav, not amoxicillin, the first-line drug for non-severe hospital-acquired pneumonia. It lists IV piperacillin with tazobactam among the options for 'Severe symptoms or signs (for example, symptoms or signs of sepsis) or at higher risk of resistance'. High-severity community-acquired pneumonia gets co-amoxiclav with clarithromycin (Table 1). So no NG250 table pairs the rule's two drugs. (2) Exact Sepsis-3 wording: qSOFA is for 'adult patients with suspected infection' in 'out-of-hospital, emergency department, or general hospital ward settings', which matches the rule's ward population, and 'the task force chose to emphasize altered mentation because it represents any Glasgow Coma Scale score less than 15'. Retained researcher notes: Seymour CW, Liu VX, Iwashyna TJ, et al. Assessment of Clinical Criteria for Sepsis: For the Third International Consensus Definitions for Sepsis and Septic Shock (Sepsis-3). JAMA 2016;315(8):762-774: '1 point each for systolic hypotension [≤100 mm Hg], tachypnea [≥22/min], or altered mentation'. Singer M, Deutschman CS, Seymour CW, et al. The Third International Consensus Definitions for Sepsis and Septic Shock (Sepsis-3). JAMA 2016;315(8):801-810: 'at least 2 of the following clinical criteria ... respiratory rate of 22/min or greater, altered mentation, or systolic blood pressure of 100 mm Hg or less', and 'The task force suggests that qSOFA criteria be used to prompt clinicians to further investigate for organ dysfunction, to initiate or escalate therapy as appropriate, and to consider referral to critical care or increase the frequency of monitoring'. The rule's move to stronger treatment loosely fits 'escalate therapy', but no source names the drugs. NG250 grades community-acquired pneumonia in hospital with CURB65 (respiratory rate 30/min or more; systolic BP below 90 or diastolic 60 mmHg or less), not qSOFA, and makes oral amoxicillin first-line for low-severity disease. Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021 (Evans L et al., Intensive Care Med 2021;47(11):1181-1247): 'We recommend against using qSOFA compared to SIRS, NEWS, or MEWS as a single screening tool for sepsis or septic shock'. To credit the borrowed criteria, the paper can write 'criteria adapted from qSOFA (re-weighted)' and cite Seymour 2016 and Singer 2016.

For acutely ill hospitalized medical patients at low risk of thrombosis (Table 2), we recommend against the use of pharmacologic prophylaxis or mechanical prophylaxis (Grade 1B).' || '2.7.1. simplifications: Seven of the 11 Padua items are left out: reduced mobility (3), already known thrombophilic condition (3), recent (≤1 month) trauma and/or surgery (2), acute myocardial infarction or ischemic stroke (1), acute infection and/or rheumatologic disorder (1), obesity (BMI ≥30) (1) and ongoing hormonal treatment (1). The four kept items keep their source points (3, 3, 1, 1) and the ≥4 cutoff.
'Heart and/or respiratory failure' is cut down to current heart failure; respiratory failure is left out.

The source definition of active cancer ('local or distant metastases and/or ... chemotherapy or radiotherapy ... in the previous 6 mo') is not given. The rule says only 'active cancer' and counts current cancer only, so a cancer described as treated, with chemotherapy or radiotherapy in the last 6 months, scores 3 under Padua but may score 0 under the rule.
'Previous VTE (with the exclusion of superficial vein thrombosis)' becomes 'a venous thromboembolism of the patient, current or previous', and the superficial vein thrombosis exclusion is not stated.
One option is picked from several: recommendation 2.3 allows LMWH, LDUH twice or three times daily, or fondaparinux. The rule names enoxaparin (an LMWH) and gives no dose.

The bleeding-risk modifiers are left out: recommendations 2.7.1 and 2.7.2 advise no anticoagulant prophylaxis, and mechanical prophylaxis instead, for increased-risk patients who are bleeding or at high bleeding risk.

The score's population limits are not stated. Barbar 2010 enrolled only patients aged 18 or over who were not pregnant, not on or needing full-dose anticoagulation, and without contraindications to pharmacological prophylaxis (recent or ongoing major bleeding, platelet count below 100 x 10^9/L, creatinine clearance below 30 mL/min).
contradictions: Default arm: for low-risk patients (Padua <4), ACCP recommendation 2.4 recommends against both pharmacologic and mechanical prophylaxis, but the rule prescribes compression stockings. ACCP suggests graduated compression stockings only for increased-risk patients who are bleeding or at high risk of major bleeding (2.7.2).

The fixed setting already scores Padua items the rule leaves out. Community-acquired pneumonia is an acute infection (1 point), and 'expected to stay in bed for several days' is reduced mobility (3 points, if bed rest is expected for at least 3 days). That gives a full Padua score of at least 4, so under the source every patient in this setting is high risk and should get anticoagulant prophylaxis (2.3, unless bleeding or at high bleeding risk, 2.7.1), whatever the four rule criteria show. The rule's stockings arm then never matches the source.

Population: the rule counts a current VTE, but Padua scores only a previous VTE, and Barbar 2010 enrolled only patients who 'were not on full-dose anticoagulant therapy, did not require it for whatever indication' (964 of 2208 eligible patients were excluded 'because of ongoing anticoagulant treatment or medical conditions requiring it'). A patient with a current VTE, which needs anticoagulant treatment, is therefore outside the population the score and ACCP's prophylaxis recommendations were built for.

ASH also suggests a parenteral anticoagulant over none for acutely ill medical patients (Recommendations 1-3) and pharmacological over mechanical prophylaxis (Recommendation 6), with no Padua cutoff. (6 cm or more).'; 'Chronic Pulmonary Disease: Moderate pulmonary disease is Dyspneic with slight activity, with or without treatment and those who are dyspneic with moderate activity despite treatment.'; 'Renal Disease: Moderate renal disease includes patients with serum creatinine of >3 mg/dl.' simplifications: Subset: CHF, MI, PVD, chronic pulmonary disease and moderate renal disease are kept; all other Charlson conditions are omitted. Age is also omitted. Sorror 2005: 'Later, Charlson added age to her weighted comorbidity scores by assigning an extra point for every decade of age starting at 50 years', citing Charlson et al., J Clin Epidemiol 1994;47:1245-1251. I did not check whether the 1987 paper itself proposed an age adjustment.

MI and PVD, two separate 1-point items in the source, are merged into one 1-point criterion. The source_comment says a case names only one of them; if both were present the source would give 2 points.

PVD is restated as 'peripheral artery disease'. In the appendix wording reproduced in protocol NCT01342367, PVD covers claudication, bypass for arterial insufficiency, gangrene, acute arterial insufficiency and untreated aneurysm of 6 cm or more.

Definitions are reduced to the diagnosis. In the reproduced appendix wording (NCT01342367), CHF means exertional or paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea with a symptomatic response to digitalis, diuretics or afterload-reducing agents. MI means one or more definite or probable infarctions, hospitalised, with electrocardiographic and/or enzyme changes.
Heart failure, MI and PAD count at any time (current or past).
Chronic pulmonary disease is represented only by current asthma, a proxy chosen by the rule's author (see contradictions).
Moderate or severe renal disease is reduced to its creatinine criterion (>3 mg/dL, current value); dialysis, transplant and uraemia are omitted.
contradictions: The asthma proxy over-includes. Every reproduction of the pulmonary definition I found requires dyspnoea. The CCI rules sheets in protocols NCT00553800 and NCT01459497 say 'symptomatic dyspnea due to chronic respiratory conditions (including asthma)'. Protocol NCT01342367 Appendix C and Kim et al. 2014 (Biomed Res Int, PMC4119725) give dyspnoea with slight activity (with or without treatment), with moderate activity despite treatment, or worse. Sorror 2005 lists asthma among comorbidities 'not found in the original CCI'. The rule scores any current asthma, and several flip lines state no dyspnoea (e.g. 'Asthma, on a daily inhaled steroid.', 'Has asthma and uses an albuterol inhaler for wheeze.'). For those, the source would score 0 where the rule scores 1. I did not see the original 1987 appendix.

Sorror 2005: Tables 1 and 4, and the sentence listing asthma among comorbidities 'not found in the original CCI'. source_title: Hematopoietic cell transplantation (HCT)-specific comorbidity index: a new tool for risk assessment before allogeneic HCT
source_org_or_authors: Sorror ML, Maris MB, Storb R, Baron F, Sandmaier BM, Maloney DG, Storer B (Blood); coding guide by Sorror ML (Blood 2013)
source_identifier: doi:10.1182/blood-2005-05-2004; PMID 15994282; PMCID PMC1895304. Coding guide: Sorror ML, 'How I assess comorbidities before hematopoietic cell transplantation', Blood 2013;121(15):2854-2863, doi:10.1182/blood-2012-09-455063, PMID 23355537, PMCID PMC3624933 (both read in full on PMC)
supporting_text: Sorror 2005, Table 4 (footnote markers removed): Cardiac: 'Coronary artery disease, congestive heart failure, myocardial infarction, or EF ≤ 50%', score 1 (CAD footnote: 'One or more vessel-coronary artery stenosis requiring medical treatment, stent, or bypass graft'). Cerebrovascular disease: 'Transient ischemic attack or cerebrovascular accident', 1. Hepatic, mild: 'Chronic hepatitis, bilirubin > ULN to 1.5 × ULN, or AST/ALT > ULN to 2.5 × ULN', 1. Peptic ulcer: 'Requiring treatment', 2. Moderate/severe hepatic: 'Liver cirrhosis, bilirubin > 1.5 × ULN, or AST/ALT > 2.5 × ULN', 3. Sorror 2005 Methods: 'all other comorbidities were assigned new weights in the HCT-CI using the original definitions in the CCI, including … peptic ulcer'. Sorror 2013: CAD 'is based on the presence of a documented diagnosis of chronic exertional angina, unstable angina, or myocardial infarction at any point in the patient's past medical history'; 'A score of 1 is assigned for cerebrovascular disease on the basis of a prior diagnosis of transient ischemic attack, subarachnoid hemorrhage, or cerebral thrombosis, embolism, or hemorrhage at any time in the past medical history.' Mild hepatic: 'elevated values of any of the 2 hepatic transaminase enzymes, ALT or AST, to values higher than the ULN and up to 2.5 times the ULN'; 'assessment of the laboratory tests (a and/or b) has to include at least 2 values per test on 2 different days within a period extending between days −24 and −10 before HCT'; 'The laboratory value closest to the landmark date should be the value used in defining the severity of hepatic comorbidity'; 'The upper limit of normal (ULN) for any of the 3 tests is determined on the basis of the reference range per the institution laboratory.' 'A score of 2 is assigned for peptic ulcer on the basis of the presence of a prior endoscopic or radiologic diagnosis of gastric or duodenal ulcer, noted in the medical record, at any point in the patient's past medical history. Patients with quiescent peptic ulcer who are receiving no treatment in the immediate period before the landmark date are assigned a score for this comorbidity if they have met the prior criteria.'
simplifications: Subset: 4 of the 17 HCT-CI comorbidities are kept; arrhythmia, diabetes, renal, pulmonary, prior solid tumour and the rest are omitted.
The cardiac item (CAD, CHF, MI or EF ≤50%; 1 point) is reduced to coronary artery disease.
Cerebrovascular disease is restated as 'stroke or TIA'. The 2013 coding also lists subarachnoid haemorrhage and cerebral thrombosis, embolism or haemorrhage.

The mild hepatic item is reduced to ALT; chronic hepatitis (2013: prior hepatitis B or C infection), bilirubin and AST are omitted. ULN is fixed at 40 U/L, whereas the source uses each laboratory's reference range.

The banded hepatic item is reduced to one band. The rule gives 1 point for any ALT above 40 U/L with no upper bound, while the source scores ALT >2.5 x ULN (here >100 U/L) as moderate/severe hepatic, 3 points. The source_comment says flip values stay at or below 100 U/L; the engine draws them from 44-58 U/L.
Lab timing: the 2013 coding needs at least 2 values on 2 different days between days -24 and -10 before HCT and uses the value closest to the landmark date. The rule uses one current value.
CAD and stroke/TIA count at any time (current or past), as in the 2013 coding. Peptic ulcer counts only when current.
contradictions: Peptic ulcer timing. The 2013 coding cited in the source_comment scores 2 for 'a prior endoscopic or radiologic diagnosis of gastric or duodenal ulcer … at any point in the patient's past medical history', including a quiescent, untreated ulcer. The 2005 paper scores peptic ulcer with the original CCI definition, reproduced in CCI rules sheets as 'Patients who have required treatment for PUD' (protocols NCT00553800, NCT01459497). The rule scores only a current ulcer. Time near-miss lines such as 'Peptic ulcer in {year}, healed on repeat endoscopy.' or 'Gastric ulcer healed after eight weeks of omeprazole.' are therefore labelled 0 by the rule but score 2 under the cited coding. The restriction is stated in the rule text ('current') and in the source_comment.

source_title: Validation and refinement of scores to predict very early stroke risk after transient ischaemic attack
source_org_or_authors: Johnston SC, Rothwell PM, Nguyen-Huynh MN, Giles MF, Elkins JS, Bernstein AL, Sidney S
supporting_text: Abstract: 'In both derivation groups, c statistics were improved for a unified score based on five factors (age >or=60 years [1 point]; blood pressure >or=140/90 mm Hg [1]; clinical features: unilateral weakness [2], speech impairment without weakness [1]; duration >or=60 min [2] or 10-59 min [1]; and diabetes [1]). This score, ABCD(2), validated well'. Item definitions as applied by Holzer et al., BMC Neurol 2010;10:50 (PMC2906428), citing Johnston et al.: 'age (≥60 years, 1 point); blood pressure on first assessment after TIA (systolic blood pressure (SBP) ≥140 mmHg or diastolic blood pressure (DBP) ≥90 mmHg, 1 point); clinical features of TIA (unilateral weakness, 2 points; speech impairment without weakness, 1 point); duration of symptoms (≥60 minutes, 2 points; 10-59 minutes, 1 point); diabetes (1 point)'.
simplifications: The clinical-features item (unilateral weakness 2, speech impairment without weakness 1) and the duration item (>= 60 min 2, 10-59 min 1) are omitted.
The blood pressure item '>= 140/90 mm Hg' (systolic >= 140 or diastolic >= 90) is reduced to systolic >= 140 mmHg. The diastolic >= 90 alternative is omitted.
Blood pressure is restated as a current value; the score uses the blood pressure at the first assessment after the TIA (as described by Holzer et al. 2010). Diabetes is restated as 'at any time'.
The risk groups are not used (0-3, 4-5, 6-7).
notes: VERIFIER: I added to supporting_text a secondary statement of the item definitions (Holzer et al. 2010). It confirms that the blood pressure item is met by systolic >= 140 OR diastolic >= 90, measured at the first assessment after the TIA. I revised the blood pressure timing simplification to match. Re-checked: Crossref and Europe PMC data (Lancet 2007;369(9558):283-292) and the abstract wording as quoted. The Lancet full text is closed access (Unpaywall) and I did not open it, so the 'first assessment' timing comes from the secondary source. Under the full ABCD2, the setting (left-arm weakness lasting 20 minutes) would earn another 2 + 1 points. The rule excludes those items explicitly, so this is not a contradiction. The simplifications are complete; I found no contradictions. The source_comment was empty.

source_title: APACHE II: a severity of disease classification system
source_org_or_authors: Knaus WA, Draper EA, Wagner DP, Zimmerman JE
supporting_text: Abstract: 'APACHE II uses a point score based upon initial values of 12 routine physiologic measurements, age, and previous health status to provide a general measure of severity of disease.' Score sheet reproduced with credit to Knaus et al., Crit Care Med 1985 (Università di Catania, 'ALLEGATO 3. APACHE 2 SCORE'); table cells as rendered: 'TEMPERATURE – rectal (C°)' +4 '≥ 41°'; 'HEART RATE (ventricular response)' +4 '≥ 180'; 'RESPIRATORY RATE – (non ventilated or ventilated)' +4 '≥ 50'; 'AGE POINTS ... ≥ 75 ... 6'. Second reproduction, Ahmed et al., J Crit Care Med (Targu Mures) 2024 (PMC11193976; cites Knaus 1985), APACHE II table: 'Temperature ... ≥ 41 / ≤ 29.9 = 4 points'; 'Heart Rate ... ≥180 / ≤ 39 = 4 points'; 'Respiratory Rate ... ≥50 / ≤ 5 = 4 points'; 'Age ... 65–74 = 5 points, >74 = 6 points'.
simplifications: Each banded item is reduced to its top band. Only temperature >= 41 C (4), heart rate >= 180/min (4), respiratory rate >= 50/min (4) and age >= 75 (6) score, and the rule says every other value scores 0. The source also scores: temperature 39-40.9 = 3, 38.5-38.9 = 1, 34-35.9 = 1, 32-33.9 = 2, 30-31.9 = 3, <= 29.9 = 4; heart rate 140-179 = 3, 110-139 = 2, 55-69 = 2, 40-54 = 3, <= 39 = 4; respiratory rate 35-49 = 3, 25-34 = 1, 10-11 = 1, 6-9 = 2, <= 5 = 4; age 45-54 = 2, 55-64 = 3, 65-74 = 5.
Rectal temperature is restated as 'temperature', with no measurement site.

Timing: the source scores the physiologic values at ICU admission (abstract: 'initial values'). MDCalc's instructions use the worst value recorded in the first 24 hours in the ICU, or the initial values. The rule uses current values.

The other acute physiology items are omitted (mean arterial pressure, oxygenation, arterial pH or HCO3, sodium, potassium, creatinine, hematocrit, white cell count, Glasgow Coma Scale), as are the chronic health points. There is no total score or mortality estimate.
notes: VERIFIER: I completed the list of omitted bands in the first simplification, checking every band against two reproductions. I reworded the timing simplification: the abstract says 'initial values', while the 'worst value in the first 24 hours' is MDCalc's instruction ('The worst values recorded during the initial 24 hours in the ICU should be used. Alternatively, the variables initially recorded during the patient's admission can be used'), not a quote from the source. I added a second reproduction to supporting_text. Re-checked: Crossref (Crit Care Med 1985;13(10):818-829, doi:10.1097/00003246-198510000-00009) and the Europe PMC abstract (PMID 3928249). The full text is closed access (Unpaywall) and I did not open it. I downloaded the Catania sheet (spinuti.unict.it/assets/files/allegato_3.pdf), which credits Knaus et al., and extracted its text. It confirms rectal temperature, the values 41°, 180 and 50 in the +4 high-abnormal column, and 6 age points for 75 and over. The ≥ glyphs are lost in text extraction, but the values sit in the +4 high column. Wikipedia's age table gives >=75 = 6. The clause 'Any other value of these items scores 0 here' openly departs from the banded points. It is a declared band reduction (simplification), not a contradiction. I found no contradictions. The source_comment was empty.

source_title: Prognostic factors in acute pancreatitis
source_org_or_authors: Blamey SL, Imrie CW, O'Neill J, Gilmour WH, Carter DC (Gut)
source_identifier: doi:10.1136/gut.25.12.1340; PMID 6510766; PMCID PMC1420197 (scanned pages read at https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1420197/)
supporting_text: Table 1 ('Basis of factor scoring systems to predict the severity of acute pancreatitis'), column 'Imrie et al (1978)', within 48 hours: 'age >55 years', 'WBC >15×10⁹/l', 'serum urea >16 mmol/l (no response to iv fluids)'; footnote: 'For either system: severe disease = three or more factors present.' Table 4 ('Significant factors in predicting severity of acute pancreatitis') lists Urea (mmol/l) '>16', WBC '>15', Age (yr) '>55'. Discussion: 'Exclusion of the aminotransferases from the original system, leaving eight individually significant risk factors, increased overall predictive value … we recommend the use of the eight factor system.' Methods: 'we have used the highest value recorded within 48 hours of admission for the serum concentrations of … urea … white blood cell count'. Abstract: 'a system using nine factors available within 48 hours of admission'.
simplifications: Subset: 3 of the 8 factors of the modified Glasgow system (9 in Imrie 1978) are kept: age, white cell count and urea. Glucose, PaO2, calcium, albumin and LDH are omitted, and so is AST/ALT from the 1978 version.
The source counts factors (severe disease = three or more present); the rule gives 1 point per factor and does not use the severity cut-off.
Units: serum urea >16 mmol/l is converted to blood urea nitrogen (16 mmol/l x 2.8 = 44.8 mg/dL) and rounded up to 'above 45 mg/dL'. See contradictions for the effect at exactly 45.
The urea qualifier '(no response to iv fluids)' is omitted.
Timing: the source counts a factor present within 48 hours of admission, using the highest urea and white cell count recorded in that window. The rule uses the current value.
contradictions: Urea cut-off rounding: the source's urea >16 mmol/l equals BUN >44.8 mg/dL, but the rule says 'above 45 mg/dL'. The engine's boundary near-miss sets BUN to exactly 45 mg/dL (about 16.1 mmol/l urea). That value meets the source factor but is labelled 0 under the rule.

Possible, superseded tier only: these cases show a flip-side white cell count or BUN from yesterday, earlier this week or last month, replaced by a default-side value today. The rule scores 0. Under the source's highest-value-within-48-hours convention, the factor is present if the earlier value falls within 48 hours of admission. The cases do not say when the patient was admitted.
notes: VERIFIER: Confirmed the bibliographic record in Europe PMC and re-read all seven PMC page images. Table 1, its footnote, Table 4, the Methods sentence and the Discussion recommendation match the quotes. Confirmed the Imrie 1978 record (Br J Surg 1978;65(5):337-341, PMID 348250, doi:10.1002/bjs.1800650514) and its abstract on https://academic.oup.com/bjs/article/65/5/337/6193027: 'at least three of a possible nine factors during the first 48 h of admission'. Changes: added two contradictions the record missed. (1) engine.py sets a 'boundary' near-miss exactly at a strict threshold, and rules_score.py gives BUN '>' 45, so every BUN boundary triplet uses BUN 45. (2) A possible timing disagreement in the superseded tier. Reworded the units and timing simplifications to match. Provenance, source and verification status are unchanged. Stating 'above 44 mg/dL' (whole numbers) would agree with the source. The age (55) and white cell count (15.0) boundary cases score 0 under both rule and source.

source_title: Predictive and associative models to identify hospitalized medical patients at risk for VTE
source_org_or_authors: Spyropoulos AC, Anderson FA, FitzGerald G, Decousus H, Pini M, Chong BH, Zotz RB, Bergmann JF, Tapson V, Froehlich JB, Monreal M, Merli GJ, Pavanello R, Turpie AGG, Nakamura M, Piovella F, Kakkar AK, Spencer FA; IMPROVE Investigators
supporting_text: Abstract: 'Factors independently associated with VTE were previous VTE, known thrombophilia, cancer, age > 60 years, lower-limb paralysis, immobilization ≥ 7 days, and admission to an ICU or coronary care unit (first four were available at admission). Points were assigned to each factor identified to give a total risk score for each patient.' Points as reproduced in Rosenberg et al., J Am Heart Assoc 2014 (PMC4338701; Spyropoulos is a co-author): 'the 7-factor IMPROVE model (previous VTE, 3 points; known thrombophilia, 2 points; lower limb paralysis, 2 points; cancer, 2 points; immobilization, 1 point; intensive care unit or coronary care unit stay, 1 point; aged >60 years, 1 point)'.
simplifications: Omitted: known thrombophilia (2), current lower-limb paralysis (2), immobilization >= 7 days (1) and ICU/CCU stay (1).

The source derives two VTE scores: a 4-factor score from the factors available at admission and a 7-factor score that adds in-hospital factors. The rule takes the 7-factor points (previous VTE 3, cancer 2, age > 60 years 1). In the 4-factor admission score, cancer scores 1 point (previous VTE 3, known thrombophilia 3, age > 60 years 1).

'Previous VTE' is restated as a VTE of the patient 'at any time (current or previous)'. The explicit 'current' takes the item beyond the source's 'previous VTE'. External validations apply the score only to admissions without VTE present on admission.
The cancer item is restated as 'active cancer'. The IMPROVEDD paper by the same group labels it 'Current cancer'.
Age > 60 years is kept. The risk categories are not used.
notes: VERIFIER: Added a simplification that the source has two IMPROVE VTE scores with different cancer points, and that the rule follows the 7-factor score. Wilkinson et al., Res Pract Thromb Haemost 2024 (PMC11215414), Table 2 gives these values in its columns 'results from Spyropoulos et al.': 'Previous VTE ... 3', 'Known thrombophilia ... 3', 'Cancer ... 1', 'Age >60 y ... 1'. The text describes this as a 0-8 point score from 4 risk factors. Alfehaid et al., Front Cardiovasc Med 2025 (PMC12833051), Table 2 gives the same 4-factor points and the 7-factor points (current malignancy 2, thrombophilia 2). The rule's 2 points for cancer match the 7-factor score (Rosenberg 2014), so this is a choice between the source's two models, not a contradiction. Note that Wilkinson 2024 uses the name 'IMPROVE-VTE risk score' for the 4-factor version, so the name is ambiguous in the literature. I also extended the 'previous VTE' simplification. Rosenberg 2014 excluded admissions with VTE present on admission, and Wilkinson 2024 computed the score only for admissions without VTE at admission. I could not confirm the original registry's own exclusion criteria. Counting a current VTE therefore goes beyond how the score is used. I kept it as a declared applicability restatement (simplification), but the authors may prefer to drop 'current or' from the rule text. Re-checked: Crossref and Europe PMC data and the abstract. The Chest article is closed access (Unpaywall), so I did not open the full text. The Rosenberg 2014 quote matches the Europe PMC full text, and Spyropoulos is its last author. Gibson et al., TH Open 2017;1(1):e56-e65 (PMC6524839) labels the items 'Previous VTE', 'Current cancer' and 'Age >60 y'. The source_comment was empty.

source_title: Definitions for sepsis and organ failure and guidelines for the use of innovative therapies in sepsis. The ACCP/SCCM Consensus Conference Committee (Chest 1992;101(6):1644-1655), Recommendation 1 and Table 1
source_org_or_authors: Bone RC, Balk RA, Cerra FB, Dellinger RP, Fein AM, Knaus WA, Schein RM, Sibbald WJ; ACCP/SCCM Consensus Conference Committee (American College of Chest Physicians/Society of Critical Care Medicine)
source_identifier: doi:10.1378/chest.101.6.1644; PMID 1303622; scanned full text read at https://confluence.cornell.edu/download/attachments/344131056/Definitions%20for%20Sepsis%20and%20Organ%20Failure%20and%20Guidelines%20for%20the%20Use%20of%20Innovative%20Therapies%20in%20Sepsis.pdf?api=v2 (Recommendation 1 on p. 1645; Table 1 on p. 1646)
supporting_text: Table 1 (p. 1646): 'Systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS) = the systemic inflammatory response to a variety of severe clinical insults. The response is manifested by two or more of the following conditions: (1) temperature >38°C or <36°C; (2) heart rate >90 beats per minute; (3) respiratory rate >20 breaths per minute or PaCO2 <32 mm Hg; and (4) white blood cell count >12,000/cu mm, <4,000/cu mm, or >10% immature (band) forms'. Recommendation 1 (p. 1645): 'This systemic inflammatory response can be seen following a wide variety of insults and includes, but is not limited to, more than one of the following clinical manifestations: (1) a body temperature greater than 38°C or less than 36°C; (2) a heart rate greater than 90 beats per minute; (3) tachypnea, manifested by a respiratory rate greater than 20 breaths per minute, or hyperventilation, as indicated by a PaCO2 of less than 32 mm Hg; and (4) an alteration in the white blood cell count, such as a count greater than 12,000/cu mm, a count less than 4,000/cu mm, or the presence of more than 10 percent immature neutrophils ("bands"). These physiologic changes should represent an acute alteration from baseline in the absence of other known causes for such abnormalities, such as chemotherapy, induced neutropenia, and leukopenia.'
simplifications: The SIRS definition ('two or more of the following conditions') is restated as 1 point per criterion; the >=2 threshold is not used.
Temperature item reduced to its upper arm (>38°C); the <36°C arm omitted.
Respiratory item reduced to respiratory rate >20/min; the PaCO2 <32 mm Hg alternative omitted.
White-cell item reduced to >12,000/cu mm; the <4,000/cu mm and >10% immature (band) forms arms omitted.
Units converted: >12,000/cu mm stated as above 12.0 x10^9/L (equivalent).

Applicability restated as 'Only current findings count'. The source's qualifier is not stated: the changes 'should represent an acute alteration from baseline in the absence of other known causes for such abnormalities, such as chemotherapy, induced neutropenia, and leukopenia'. A current abnormal value with another known cause counts under the rule.
notes: VERIFIER: Re-downloaded and read the cited scanned article. Table 1 on p. 1646 (rendered and viewed) matches the quoted SIRS definition and thresholds exactly. Changed supporting_text: the researcher's 'Text:' sentence ('Also, the physiologic changes measured should represent an acute alteration from baseline...') comes from the sepsis paragraph (Recommendation 3, p. 1646), not the SIRS one. I replaced it with the SIRS-specific Recommendation 1 passage (p. 1645, rendered and checked against the scan), which also names other causes such as chemotherapy. The applicability simplification was updated to match. Also confirmed the parallel publication in PubMed: Crit Care Med 1992;20(6):864-874, PMID 1597042, no authors listed; DOI 10.1097/00003246-199206000-00025 per OpenAlex; text not opened. No contradictions found. source_comment was empty.

source_title: Lipitor 10 mg film-coated tablets – Summary of Product Characteristics (UK), section 4.3; NICE NG238 Cardiovascular disease: risk assessment and reduction, including lipid modification; NICE TA385 Ezetimibe for treating primary heterozygous-familial and non-familial hypercholesterolaemia
source_org_or_authors: Viatris Products Limited (SmPC, PL 46302/0298); National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)
source_year: SmPC text revised 11/2025; NG238 published 14 Dec 2023; TA385 published 24 Feb 2016
source_identifier: https://www.medicines.org.uk/emc/product/1059/smpc; https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng238/chapter/Recommendations; https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ta385/chapter/1-Recommendations
supporting_text: Lipitor SmPC 4.3: "Lipitor is contraindicated in patients: ... with active liver disease or unexplained persistent elevations of serum transaminases exceeding 3 times the upper limit of normal". NICE NG238 1.6.7: "Offer atorvastatin 20 mg for the primary prevention of CVD to people who have a 10-year QRISK3 score of 10% or more." NG238 1.5.6: "Do not routinely exclude from statin treatment people who have liver transaminase levels that are raised but are less than 3 times the upper limit of normal." NICE TA385 1.2: "Ezetimibe monotherapy is recommended as an option for treating primary (heterozygous-familial or non-familial) hypercholesterolaemia in adults in whom initial statin therapy is contraindicated."
simplifications: 'Unexplained persistent elevations of serum transaminases exceeding 3 times the upper limit of normal' is reduced to one current ALT value above 120 U/L. The 3x ULN multiple becomes a fixed 120 U/L, which implies a ULN of 40 U/L (laboratory ULNs vary). 'Persistent' and 'unexplained' are dropped, AST is omitted, and 'active liver disease' is omitted.
Primary-prevention eligibility (QRISK3 ≥10%) and dose (atorvastatin 20 mg) are not stated.
Alternative fixed to ezetimibe monotherapy, which TA385 lists as 'an option'.
Other atorvastatin contraindications omitted (hypersensitivity; pregnancy, breast-feeding, and women of child-bearing potential not using contraception; glecaprevir/pibrentasvir).
notes: VERIFIER: Re-opened the Lipitor 10 mg SmPC (Viatris Products Limited, PL 46302/0298, revision 11/2025). The 4.3 wording matches, including the glecaprevir/pibrentasvir contraindication. Re-opened NICE NG238 (published 14 December 2023; 1.5.6 and 1.6.7 match) and NICE TA385 (published 24 February 2016; 1.2 matches). The US LIPITOR SPL (setid a60cc18b-0631-4cf0-b021-9f52224ece65, effective 2024-04-15) lists 'Acute liver failure or decompensated cirrhosis' as its hepatic contraindication and says 'Consider testing liver enzymes before initiating therapy'. The rule follows UK labelling. No field needed correction. Added note: the alt-tier variant (ALT > 80 U/L) conflicts with NG238 1.5.6 for ALT 81-120 U/L, which is raised but below 3x ULN on the same 40 U/L assumption, and no source was found for it. The alt tier is a deliberate counterfactual rule text, so this is recorded here and not as a contradiction of the main rule.

source_title: Clinical practice guideline for the diagnosis and management of group A streptococcal pharyngitis: 2012 update by the Infectious Diseases Society of America
source_org_or_authors: Shulman ST, Bisno AL, Clegg HW, Gerber MA, Kaplan EL, Lee G, Martin JM, Van Beneden C; Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDSA)
supporting_text: Recommendation 8: "Based on their narrow spectrum of activity, infrequency of adverse reactions, and modest cost, penicillin or amoxicillin is the recommended drug of choice for those non-allergic to these agents (strong, high)." Recommendation 9: "Treatment of GAS pharyngitis in penicillin-allergic individuals should include a first generation cephalosporin (for those not anaphylactically sensitive) for 10 days, clindamycin or clarithromycin for 10 days, or azithromycin for 5 days (strong, moderate)." Evidence summary: "A 10-day course of an oral cephalosporin is recommended for most penicillin-allergic individuals (Table 2)." ... "An oral macrolide (erythromycin or clarithromycin) or azalide (azithromycin at a dose of 12 mg/kg/day, up to a maximum of 500 mg) is also reasonable for patients allergic to penicillin."
simplifications: Default fixed to amoxicillin; the source recommends penicillin or amoxicillin.

Alternative fixed to azithromycin. Recommendation 9 lists a first-generation cephalosporin (only for patients without anaphylactic-type allergy), clindamycin, clarithromycin or azithromycin. The evidence summary recommends a cephalosporin for most penicillin-allergic individuals, calls a macrolide or azithromycin 'also reasonable', and notes macrolide resistance of about 5%-8% in most US areas.
Type of penicillin allergy (anaphylactic vs non-anaphylactic) is not distinguished; any penicillin allergy triggers the switch.
Doses and durations omitted (10 days for penicillin/amoxicillin and 5 days for azithromycin in the source).
Applicability restated: only a current penicillin allergy counts (counts_past=false); the source does not address resolved or de-labelled allergies.
Diagnosis taken as confirmed (rapid antigen test positive in the setting); the guideline's testing criteria are not part of the rule.
notes: VERIFIER: Confirmed via NCBI E-utilities that PMID 22965026 = doi:10.1093/cid/cis629 = PMC7108032. Both quoted recommendations appear verbatim in the PMC full text ('should include' in the summary, 'may include' in the body). Changes: (1) Added to supporting_text and simplification 2 what the evidence summary says: a cephalosporin is recommended for most penicillin-allergic patients, a macrolide or azithromycin is 'also reasonable', and macrolide resistance is a concern. Azithromycin is still a listed option, so this is not a contradiction. (2) PubMed does not call PMID 23091044 an executive summary. It is a 4-page print article with the same title (Clin Infect Dis 2012;55(10):1279-82, doi:10.1093/cid/cis847). Both records carry an erratum for a dosage error (Clin Infect Dis 2014;58(10):1496); it does not affect the rule because doses are omitted. (3) Replaced the secondary reports on the 2025 update with the primary record: Linder JA et al., '2025 Clinical Practice Guideline Update by the Infectious Diseases Society of America on Group A Streptococcal Pharyngitis: Risk Assessment Using Clinical Scoring Systems in Children and Adults', Clin Infect Dis 2026;82(Suppl 3):i97-i104, doi:10.1093/cid/ciaf668, PMID 41343363 (abstract opened). It was received 11 Nov 2025 and indexed 4 Dec 2025, so the 'October 2025' date is not supported. Its abstract calls it the first part of an update; it covers only clinical scoring to decide whom to test. No treatment part was found in PubMed on 2 Oct 2026, so the 2012 treatment recommendations are the latest IDSA treatment text found.
